title: Free Cash Flow - a closer reading
subtitle: FCF = OCF − CapEx, NOPAT and working capital
openingQuestion: What is the shortest common definition of FCF?
explanation: Free cash flow is the cash left over once the business has funded its operations and the investment it needs to maintain or expand. It is the money the company is genuinely free to use - to pay a dividend, buy back shares, repay debt or accumulate - without damaging the core business.

realWorldExample.company: VND 500bn of profit, almost no free cash flow
realWorldExample.description: A business reports VND 500bn of profit. Add back VND 200bn of depreciation and operating cash is 700bn - which sounds strong. But to hold that growth rate it spent VND 450bn on fixed assets that year and let another 200bn get stuck in receivables and inventory as revenue swelled. Free cash flow comes to VND 50bn, a tenth of the profit figure. This does not mean the business is weak: it means the entire profit is being reinvested, and the next question is what that reinvestment earns. Every growing business passes through this phase; the problem only appears when it never ends.

quiz.question: What does sustained positive FCF usually indicate?
options: The business no longer has any bank borrowing outstanding
The business is cutting its investment spending too far
The business has the highest gross margin in its sector
The business is better able to fund itself
quiz.explanation: Positive FCF means the business generates real cash after the investment it needs.

quiz.question: Two companies in the same sector have equal EBITDA, but company A has far higher FCF than company B. What is the most likely reason?
options: Company A needs less CapEx or working capital to operate
Company A has much lower interest costs than company B
Company A recognises revenue on a different basis from company B
Company A is on a tax incentive and so retains more
quiz.explanation: EBITDA deducts neither CapEx nor the change in working capital, while FCF deducts both. Two businesses with the same EBITDA but one needing far more capital to sustain its growth - an asset-heavy sector, say - will have very different FCF. That is why FCF is generally treated as the truer measure of economic value.

quiz.question: Two businesses both have EBITDA of 500bn and OCF of 400bn, but CapEx of 80bn and 250bn respectively. How far apart is their FCF?
options: No difference, since their EBITDA is the same
320bn against 150bn, a gap of 170bn
500bn against 500bn
80bn against 250bn
quiz.explanation: FCF = OCF − CapEx: 400 − 80 = 320 and 400 − 250 = 150. Identical EBITDA but different capital intensity leaves a large gap in the cash that is genuinely free.

quiz.question: Why can comparing two businesses on EBITDA alone mislead you?
options: Because EBITDA is heavily affected by depreciation policy
Because EBITDA is not defined by any accounting standard
Because EBITDA does not deduct CapEx or the change in working capital
Because EBITDA moves with the company's capital structure
quiz.explanation: This is exactly why FCF is generally seen as the more honest measure of real economic value - it accounts for the burden of necessary investment, which EBITDA ignores.

quiz.question: Why should maintenance capex and expansion capex be separated when you assess free cash flow?
options: Because maintenance is tax deductible while expansion is not
Because accounting standards require the two to be presented on separate lines
Because expansion capex is excluded from investing cash flow for the period
Because only maintenance is compulsory - expansion can be stopped if needed
quiz.explanation: A business with negative free cash flow because it is building another plant is quite different from one that is negative because ageing machinery constantly has to be replaced. The statements do not split the two, so the analyst has to estimate - depreciation is the usual proxy for the maintenance portion.

keyTakeaways: FCF is the cash left after the investment the business needs
Both OCF and CapEx have to be read
FCF is the closest thing to the economic value created

summary.keyIdea: FCF is the cash left after the investment the business needs
summary.commonMistake: Easy to overlook: both OCF and CapEx have to be read
summary.action: FCF is the closest thing to the economic value created

sections.text: EBITDA is the familiar measure, but two companies in the same sector with identical EBITDA can still be in very different financial health - and free cash flow is where that difference shows up.

Free cash flow is the cash left over once the business has funded its operations and the investment it needs to maintain or grow - the money it is genuinely free to use for dividends, buybacks, debt repayment or accumulation. EBITDA deducts neither CapEx nor the change in working capital, while FCF deducts both: two companies with equal EBITDA, one of which has to commit far more capital to sustain its growth in an asset-heavy sector, will have very different free cash flow.

items: FCF is what is left once the necessary CapEx is taken out of operating cash flow
EBITDA ignores CapEx and working capital, so it can mislead when used on its own
Sustained positive FCF shows the business can fund itself without borrowing more

sections.title: From EBITDA to free cash flow
sections.equation: FCF = Operating cash flow − Capital expenditure (CapEx)

example.title: Two businesses with the same EBITDA
example.calculation: Business A: OCF 400, CapEx 80 · Business B: OCF 400, CapEx 250
example.explanation: They generate the same operating cash flow, but B has to reinvest three times as much to maintain and grow - the hallmark of an asset-heavy sector such as heavy manufacturing or telecoms. The cash genuinely free for dividends, buybacks or debt repayment is far lower at B, even though the two have the same EBITDA.

items: EBITDA does not deduct CapEx, so two businesses with the same EBITDA but different capital intensity are in very different financial health.
EBITDA does not reflect the change in working capital - a business whose receivables and inventory are growing fast can show attractive EBITDA while its actual cash does not rise with it.
EBITDA is usually used for valuation multiples because it compares easily across different capital structures, and that is precisely why it is easily abused to hide the real investment burden.

sections.label: Maintenance capex and expansion capex
sections.text: Not all CapEx is alike. Maintenance capex is only enough to keep the existing assets running; expansion capex is aimed at adding capacity or opening a new market. At a mature business, separating the two shows much more clearly what the 'real' free cash flow would be if the company only had to maintain rather than expand.

lines: EBITDA tells you how much the business earns before the adjustments.
FCF tells you how much cash it actually HAS LEFT once the necessary investment is done - and that is the real economic value.

practicePrompt.question: What is the formula for Free Cash Flow to the Firm (FCFF), starting from operating cash flow (OCF)?
options: FCFF = OCF less the CapEx incurred during the period
FCFF = Profit after tax + Total borrowings
FCFF = Net revenue − Cost of goods sold
FCFF = Closing cash / Share capital
practicePrompt.explanation: Free Cash Flow to the Firm (FCFF) = OCF − CapEx. It is the cash actually left for both lenders and shareholders once the fixed asset base has been maintained and expanded.
